title: What to keep from Seneca
hook: time, friendship, reading, calm, and honesty about failure

segments.voice: Yesterday: the death in the bath, and the people who stayed. Your line was beside him. Whose side were you on, even for a minute? Day five hundred eighteen.

When you move house, there's a moment with every box: keep, or let go? Not everything from the old place fits in the new one. We're nearly done with Seneca. Almost ninety days of his letters and essays, and this week alone took us through gifts given and received, a grieving mother, a shameful letter from exile, a better letter to his own mother, and the long evening of his death. Before we move on, it's time to pack. Today: what to keep from Seneca.
screen: `KEEP, OR LET GO?` → `NEARLY NINETY DAYS OF SENECA.` → `WHAT TO KEEP.`

segments.voice: Here are five candidates. You'll keep three. First, time. The very first letter: "Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time." Everything else can be taken, Seneca says, and yet time is the thing we let leak away most carelessly. Second, friendship. Seneca's whole body of letters is one long friendship with Lucilius. He passes on an old line from the philosopher Hecato: if you want to be loved, love. And this week added two more pictures of it: giving freely and forgetting, and receiving gladly, so the gift lands. Third, reading. Not everywhere at once. Stay with a few good writers until they become part of you, he said early on, because a mind that's everywhere is nowhere. Fourth, calm. On Anger gave us the plainest cure: delay. Let the first rush pass, and then judge. Fifth, honesty about failure. He told Lucilius he was not wise, only less bad each day. He admitted seasickness, tears, mistakes. And this week we saw a failure he didn't admit in the letter itself: flattery from exile. Maybe that's the strongest reason to keep this one. Seneca is the teacher who shows you that a person can be both wise and compromised, and still be worth reading. Which three will you keep? There's no right answer. Some people keep time, because they're always behind. Some keep friendship, because they've been lonely. Some keep honesty about failure, because they're tired of pretending. Choose the three that would change an ordinary Tuesday.
screen: `TIME: NOTHING ELSE IS OURS.` · `FRIENDSHIP: TO BE LOVED, LOVE.` · `READING AND CALM.` · `HONESTY ABOUT FAILURE.` · then, large: `THREE KEEPERS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Picture five boxes in front of you, each with a label. Time. Friendship. Reading. Calm. Honesty about failure. Pick up each one, slowly, and feel how heavy it is in your life right now. Which ones do you actually need? Choose three. Set the other two down gently; they're not gone, they'll wait. Hold your three for a while. The bell holds the time.
What to keep from Seneca. Five candidates: time, friendship, reading, calm, honesty about failure. Choose three to carry on. Today's word.
screen: `WHAT TO KEEP FROM SENECA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: three keepers. Write your three on something you'll see tomorrow, a note, a phone screen, the inside of a book. Day five hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Many readers of Seneca carry a few of his themes with them rather than his whole system: guarding time, tending friendships, reading deeply, delaying anger, and admitting their own failures.

original.note: Latin: time. The first keeper, from Seneca's very first letter.

what it means: choosing what you'll actually carry, because nobody carries a whole philosopher.
what a scholar hears: Seneca himself recommended this: in Letter 2 he urges taking one thought from each day's reading to digest.
